title: Tiny-frame adaptor experiment notes
content:
Purpose and context:

This doc captures an experimental approach we ran in Q4 to reduce tail latency and improve client ergonomics for partial/structured outputs in hosted streaming calls while preserving a clear contract for tool invocations. It is intentionally lightweight — notes, observations, and concrete next steps for product + SDK owners.

Why we tried a 'tiny-frame adaptor':
- Problem: many customers observe high variance when streaming heavy-tool-augmented responses (tool calls + large JSON blobs). Client SDKs either buffer too long or attempt to parse half-formed structures.
- Goal: enable an efficient streaming surface where small, semantically meaningful frames are emitted frequently so clients can hydrate UI state and trigger tool-side actions earlier, without coupling clients to full schema boundaries.
- Hypothesis: emitting microframes (<= 512 bytes) containing semantically tagged fragments and soft-commit markers will reduce perceived latency and simplify client-side replay/resume logic.

Key concepts introduced in the experiment:
- microframe: a compact streaming chunk with a header and a payload. Header fields are minimal: frame_id, seq, type, watermark_token, partial_path_hint. Payload is opaque bytes or small JSON fragments.
- soft-commit: a best-effort signal that tells clients that a sub-tree of the structured output is unlikely to change (can be rendered). Not a strong durability guarantee — presence of soft-commit improves UX but server may still deliver later corrections (with correction frames).
- slot hedging: runtime policy where the server tries to fill a small number of parallel generation 'slots' for tool calls so the overall stream continues emitting microframes even when a long-running tool call is in-flight.
- compact-envelope: a thin wrapper for structured outputs (e.g., partial JSON) with a short schema id and a version tag to aid lightweight validation in clients.

API and SDK ergonomics changes we trialed:
- New streaming envelope: we introduced an additional 'frame' boundary in the streaming protocol (delta messages were unchanged). Clients can opt-in via an Accept header (Accept: application/x-redwood-microframe).
- Two client modes: "eager" (display partial fragments as they arrive) and "stable" (wait for soft-commit for a subtree before rendering). Default remains stable for backwards compatibility.
- Tool-call handshake: microframes may carry a tool-candidate tag. When a microframe indicates an upcoming tool call, the SDK can pre-open a provisional tool channel (lightweight local queue) so the tool invocation completes quickly once the canonical tool payload arrives.
- Resume semantics: streams carry watermark_token at frame level. If a connection drops, clients can reconnect and request resume from the last acknowledged watermark_token. The server will attempt to rehydrate KV cache to the same generation state.

Observations from the experiment runs (internal lab + two customer pilots):
- Perceived time-to-first-action improved 22–38% on pilot apps that used eager mode.
- Bandwidth overhead: microframes added ~4–8% extra bytes across sessions due to headers and more frequent small payloads. Acceptable for mobile use-cases tested, but needs monitoring for low-bandwidth customers.
- Client complexity: SDK needed ~180 lines of new code to support microframe parsing and merge heuristics. Integrating soft-commit required explicit merge conflict resolution rules but was manageable.
- Edge cases: nested large attachments (base64 images) still cause large pauses. We recommend special-casing attachments into separate attachment frames and not attempting to microframe them.
- Tool latency interplay: slot hedging reduced end-to-end stall time but sometimes introduced duplicate tool attempts that had to be deduplicated by a tool-id returned by the server.

Structured output implications and recommendations:
- Compact schema id: publish a concise schema registry for microframe fragments. SDKs use the id to apply local validations and safe-merging. Registry entries should be tiny strings like 'rj-v1:summary'.
- Merge semantics: define three simple resolutions for partial merges: replace (fragment replaces existing subtree), append (concatenate arrays of deltas), and annotate (attach corrections as annotations). Keep default conservative (annotate).
- Correction frames: allow the server to send correction frames that reference affected frame_ids and watermark_tokens. SDK must be able to patch rendered state with minimal flicker (fade/replace transitions).

Operational and observability notes:
- Telemetry: emit frame-level metrics (frames/sec, avg frame size, correction-rate, %soft-commits). Add route-level SLOs for correction-rate: target < 5% for stable render paths.
- Cost: microframes slightly increase token accounting complexity — we tracked ~5% token inflation on pilots. Billing models should continue to bill by tokens at the model layer; microframe headers are accounted to operational overhead for now.
- Rollout gating: use canary percentage + feature-flagged SDK opt-ins. Start with internal customers and a small pilot bucket.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Strong vs soft commit: should we provide an option for strong commits for enterprise customers that want deterministic outputs? Strong commits require extra work to flush backend caches and guarantee idempotent tool semantics.
- Backcompat: how long do we support stable default before switching defaults for new SDKs? Suggest: keep stable default for 12 months and iterate on telemetry.
- Attachment strategy: do we mandate separate attachment frames (recommended) or allow in-band microfragmenting (not recommended due to complexity)?
- Deduplication surface: which ids do we require for dedupe (client-provided request id, server tool invocation id)? Proposed: require server tool_invocation_id for dedupe and accept optional client_request_id for correlation.

Concrete next steps (short-term):
1) Collate telemetry for next 6 weeks from pilots (HAPI-1298). Liam will deliver a metrics dashboard prototype (due 2026-02-28).
2) Document a compact schema registry format and sample entries (Sofia + product writer, due 2026-03-07).
3) Add an attachment-frame proposal for special-casing large blobs and finalize canonical header (Ravi to draft PR, due 2026-03-14).
4) Prepare SDK beta: JavaScript + Swift bindings with microframe opt-in flag. Target internal devs by 2026-03-21.

Longer-term considerations:
- Consider a stronger consistency mode for Dedicated/Private customers where soft-commit semantics are replaced by sync commit and tool call idempotency guarantees.
- Explore server-side heuristics to decide eager vs stable per-client (client hints + historical session behavior).
- Quantize streaming billing: consider a small per-frame operational surcharge for microframes for very high-frequency streams to avoid cost leakage.

Appendix: quick sketch of microframe header (informal)
- frame_id: short hex (client-visible)
- seq: integer (monotonic per-session)
- type: fragment | soft-commit | correction | attachment | tool-candidate
- schema_id: short string or empty
- watermark_token: short opaque token for resume
- partial_path_hint: JSON-Pointer-like short hint (optional)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working experiment doc; feedback sought on merge semantics and whether to make microframes opt-in indefinitely (feature flag) vs experimental-only.
- If you have strong opinions about strong-commit behavior, please file HAPI-1306 with concrete enterprise use-cases.

End of notes.
